decide.title: How I Decide
decide.intro: Five steps. Each links to where I actually used it.

steps.title: Check whether the problem is the problem
steps.body: Briefs arrive pre-framed. The first job is finding out whether the framing survives contact with users.
steps.linkText: Uber: the brief said universal, research said concentrated

steps.title: Work out what evidence I actually have
steps.body: Primary, secondary, or my own reasoning. Labelling this honestly changes what I'm allowed to conclude.
steps.linkText: OutLoud: 42 survey responses that didn't match my own target persona

steps.title: Decide, and name what it costs
steps.body: Every choice removes options. The ones worth writing down are the ones where I can say what I gave up.
steps.linkText: Emburse: choosing integration depth over the obvious wedge

steps.title: Build only what serves the core loop
steps.body: Features are cheap to imagine and expensive to maintain. Most of what I cut from OutLoud was cheap to build.
steps.linkText: OutLoud: what I deliberately didn't ship

steps.title: Define the measurement before the result exists
steps.body: Choosing a metric you can't game is harder than hitting one you can.

background.title: Background
background.subtitle: The Short Version
background.intro: Three things that didn't look connected until they did.
paragraphs: I studied computer engineering at Mumbai University and graduated in 2024. Somewhere in there a friend and I noticed our area had barbershops for men and parlours for women, but no unisex salon with decent hygiene. We opened one in 2023 and I still run it. I joined Ampcus Tech in Thane as an intern in November 2025 and moved into a business analyst role there in January 2026, working on requirements, user interviews, SQL and UAT.
Looked at as a CV, that's three unrelated things and an obvious question about why I keep switching.

Looked at from the inside, it's the same question three times. What do people actually need, what stops them getting it, and can you deliver it with the resources you've got. Engineering gave me the technical half. The salon gave me customers, pricing, and every constraint at once. The BA role gave me stakeholders and the discipline of writing requirements someone else has to build from.
Product management is where all three stop being separate skills.
